title: 2 Samuel 21:1–14
context: Part of the closing appendix to 2 Samuel. A three-year famine is traced to Saul’s attempt to destroy the Gibeonites, whom Israel had sworn to spare (Joshua 9). At the Gibeonites’ demand, seven of Saul’s descendants are executed; Rizpah keeps vigil over the bodies, David gives honorable burial to them and to Saul and Jonathan, and afterward God answers prayer for the land.

verses.text: There was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year; and David sought the face of the LORD. The LORD said, “It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he put the Gibeonites to death.”
verses.arminianNotes: A three-year famine leads David to seek the LORD, who says, “It is for Saul, and for his bloody house.” Arminian readers see God holding Israel accountable for a real breach of covenant faithfulness, and a king responding rightly by seeking him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence behind the famine and his word explaining it. Many in this tradition stress that national sin was not forgotten with time; the narrative presents bloodguilt as something God himself addresses.

verses.text: The king called the Gibeonites and said to them (now the Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel, but of the remnant of the Amorites, and the children of Israel had sworn to them; and Saul sought to kill them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah);
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator explains that Israel had sworn to the Gibeonites, yet Saul sought to kill them “in his zeal.” Arminian readers see Saul’s misplaced zeal breaking the oath recorded in Joshua 9:15–20, with serious consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the oath of Joshua 9 as binding on later generations. Saul’s attack is not narrated elsewhere, and readers in this tradition generally take the verse as the narrator’s explanation rather than adding details the text does not give.

verses.text: and David said to the Gibeonites, “What should I do for you? And with what should I make atonement, that you may bless the LORD’s inheritance?”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks, “What should I do for you? And with what should I make atonement?” Arminian readers see David seeking to repair a wrong done to people outside Israel, honoring their standing under the oath.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David seeking atonement so the Gibeonites may “bless the LORD’s inheritance.” Many in this tradition note the language of atonement while recognizing that the remedy chosen here raises hard questions.

verses.text: The Gibeonites said to him, “It is no matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house; neither is it for us to put any man to death in Israel.” He said, “I will do for you whatever you say.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Gibeonites refuse “silver or gold,” and say it is not for them “to put any man to death in Israel.” Arminian readers see the injured party declining a payment and deferring to the king’s authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Gibeonites framing the matter as bloodguilt rather than compensation. Numbers 35:33 is often cited by interpreters for the idea that shed blood defiles the land, though the passage itself does not cite it.

verses.text: They said to the king, “The man who consumed us and who plotted against us, that we should be destroyed from remaining in any of the borders of Israel,
verses.arminianNotes: They describe Saul as “The man who consumed us and who plotted against us.” Arminian readers see the Gibeonites voicing a real grievance about attempted destruction of their people, which the narrative takes seriously.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the grievance is presented in the Gibeonites’ own words. Readers in this tradition generally avoid reconstructing the events beyond what the speech and verse 2 actually report.

verses.text: let seven men of his sons be delivered to us, and we will hang them up to the LORD in Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD.” The king said, “I will give them.”
verses.arminianNotes: They ask for seven of Saul’s sons to “hang them up to the LORD in Gibeah of Saul,” and David agrees. Arminian readers find this demand deeply troubling and note that the text records it without explaining how God evaluates every part of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the difficulty. Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids putting children to death for their fathers’ sins, and interpreters in this tradition differ on how to relate that law to this case of royal bloodguilt.

verses.text: But the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the LORD’s oath that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.
verses.arminianNotes: David spares Mephibosheth “because of the LORD’s oath” between David and Jonathan. Arminian readers see David keeping his own covenant word even while addressing Saul’s broken oath to the Gibeonites.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant faithfulness at work, recalling the oath of 1 Samuel 20 and the kindness of 2 Samuel 9. The contrast highlights how seriously oaths sworn in the LORD’s name are treated in this chapter.

verses.text: But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Merab the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite.
verses.arminianNotes: David takes Rizpah’s two sons and Merab’s five sons. Arminian readers see the human cost named plainly, as mothers lose their sons for the sins of a king who is already dead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrative refusing to soften the loss. The WEB prints “Merab” here and does not mark a variant, and readers in this tradition generally do not build conclusions on details the text leaves unexplained.

verses.text: He delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites; and they hanged them on the mountain before the LORD, and all seven of them fell together. They were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, at the beginning of barley harvest.
verses.arminianNotes: The seven are hanged “before the LORD” at the beginning of barley harvest. Arminian readers see a grim event recorded soberly, without the narrator stating that God commanded the specific method.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the text reports the execution and its timing without commentary. Many readers in this tradition treat the passage as describing what happened rather than prescribing a pattern for later practice.

verses.text: Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water poured on them from the sky. She allowed neither the birds of the sky to rest on them by day, nor the animals of the field by night.
verses.arminianNotes: Rizpah spreads sackcloth on the rock and guards the bodies from birds and animals “from the beginning of harvest until water poured on them from the sky.” Arminian readers see grief and faithful love that refuse to abandon the dead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Rizpah’s vigil as an act of costly devotion and dignity. Deuteronomy 21:22–23 addresses bodies left hanging, and interpreters in this tradition discuss its relation to this scene without agreeing on one explanation.

verses.text: David was told what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done.
verses.arminianNotes: David is told what Rizpah has done. Arminian readers see a mother’s silent faithfulness moving the king to act, showing how the courage of one grieving woman can change the course of events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Rizpah’s vigil as the turning point in the narrative. Readers in this tradition often note that her quiet witness, not royal planning, prompts the honorable burial that follows.

verses.text: So David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh Gilead, who had stolen them from the street of Beth Shan, where the Philistines had hanged them in the day that the Philistines killed Saul in Gilboa;
verses.arminianNotes: David retrieves the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh Gilead, who had taken them from Beth Shan. Arminian readers see David honoring Saul’s house after the execution, in response to Rizpah’s example.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrative recalling 1 Samuel 31:10–13. David’s action extends respect to Saul and Jonathan, and readers in this tradition see it as restoring dignity to the royal family.

verses.text: and he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son. They also gathered the bones of those who were hanged.
verses.arminianNotes: The bones of Saul and Jonathan are brought up, and the bones of those who were hanged are gathered. Arminian readers see the executed sons given the same care as Saul and Jonathan, honoring Rizpah’s devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the gathering of the bones as an act of honor. The verse joins the seven with Saul and Jonathan, so that they are not left as outcasts.

verses.text: They buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son in the country of Benjamin in Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father; and they performed all that the king commanded. After that, God answered prayer for the land.
verses.arminianNotes: They bury the bones in the tomb of Kish, “After that, God answered prayer for the land.” Arminian readers note the text reports God’s response after the burial, without saying God approved every part of the process.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the closing note carefully. It states that God answered prayer after these events, and many in this tradition caution against inferring more about divine approval than the narrator actually says.
